claim: 2Captcha's Fingerprint API only supplies values to report (GPU name, user agent, canvas hash); it cannot make our hardware draw different pixels.
boat.dev VMs render canvas/WebGL in software (llvmpipe) because they have no GPU, and that is a known server tell.
boat.dev VMs probably draw the same canvas/WebGL image across the fleet.
boat.dev is a good host (separate machine, cookies, disk, snapshots per account) but not a convincing consumer device.
boat.dev costs about $1-2 per account per month at about 1 hour of use per account per day.
Given matt's constraints (in Vietnam, no physical hardware, cost and reliability first, scale to hundreds of thousands of accounts), a real cheap physical device per account is still the best option.
Given matt's constraints, running the accounts on this one PC as is is still the second best option.
Given matt's constraints, boat.dev VM per account wins only on scalability and is otherwise a weak option.
There is no public evidence that Meta links Marketplace accounts by canvas hash.
The bigger detection risk is the contradiction (spoofed GPU name versus real pixels), not a shared canvas hash.
A canvas hash shared with thousands of owners of the same chip can read as same hardware rather than same person.
Pinning each account's reported GPU to this PC's real chip family (Radeon 780M / RTX 4060 under ANGLE) is the right first step for Sunday.
Only a few accounts should run on this one PC.
As the operation grows, a cheap used phone or mini PC per account (or per 2-3 accounts) at about $3-6 per month is the right scaling path for matt.
If a boat trial shows matching pixel hashes or an llvmpipe renderer, Facebook sessions should stay off boat and boat should only run log-cli and non-Facebook work.
matt should not buy the 2Captcha Fingerprint API or the 2Captcha Browser API, nor add random canvas noise.
